rules.explanation: The library can run programs on the machine it is loaded on. A build tool or a process manager does this for a reason, anything else deserves a look.
Native code runs outside the JVM's checks and cannot be reviewed from the jar.
Code that is not in the jar can be loaded this way, so reading the jar does not show what runs.
A script engine runs text as code. Check where that text comes from.
A lookup with an attacker-controlled name can load remote code, as Log4Shell showed.
Deserializing untrusted data can run code through gadget chains in the classpath.
The library reaches the network on its own terms, outside any HTTP client you configure.

rules.summary: Contains an address on a host that is not trusted
rules.explanation: A library that talks to a fixed host can leak data or fetch code. Add the host to trustedHosts once you know why it is there.

rules.summary: Contains markers of a crypto miner
rules.explanation: Mining pools and miner names have no place in a library.

rules.summary: Contains markers of a reverse shell
rules.explanation: Reverse shells and raw /dev/tcp paths are how an attacker gets a shell on a build machine.

rules.summary: Pipes a download into a shell
rules.explanation: Running what was just downloaded executes code nobody reviewed.
Encoding a command hides it from review, which is rarely an accident.

rules.summary: Contains a string that looks encrypted or packed
rules.explanation: Long random-looking strings can be keys, or payloads hidden from review.

rules.summary: Uses a character that reorders text
rules.explanation: Bidirectional controls make text read differently from what runs, as in Trojan Source.
Invisible characters hide data or make two names look the same.
Tag characters are invisible and carry hidden text, which is used to smuggle instructions.
These characters have no meaning of their own and are used as a hidden payload carrier.
A word that mixes Latin with Cyrillic or Greek looks like another name.
An entry with '..' overwrites files outside the target directory when it is extracted.

rules.summary: An entry has an absolute path
rules.explanation: An absolute path overwrites any file the extracting user can write.

rules.summary: An entry has an overlong name
rules.explanation: Very long names are used to confuse tools that read archives.
Tools disagree on which of two equal names wins, so a reviewer may read another file than the JVM loads.

rules.summary: Two entries differ only in case
rules.explanation: On a case-insensitive filesystem one entry silently replaces the other.
A dotfile script in a jar has no reason to be there and is easily overlooked.
Native code cannot be reviewed from the jar and runs outside the JVM's checks.
A nested jar hides its content from tools that read only the outer one. Kreate inspects it as well.

rules.summary: The archive could not be read
rules.explanation: A jar that fails strict reading may be crafted to look different to different tools.

rules.summary: A class file could not be read
rules.explanation: A broken class cannot be loaded, so its presence is either damage or an attempt to confuse scanners.
An annotation processor runs inside the compiler with the build's privileges.

rules.summary: Runs as a compiler or KSP plugin
rules.explanation: A compiler plugin runs inside the compiler and can change the code it compiles.
A Gradle plugin runs inside the build with all of its privileges.
An agent can rewrite any class that is loaded.

rules.summary: Adds to the classpath through its manifest
rules.explanation: Class-Path entries pull in more code than the dependency declares.

rules.summary: Ships a class in a platform package
rules.explanation: A class in java/, kotlin/ or org/gradle/ from another library can replace the real one.
The findings of this module together reach inspection { failScore }. Review them, then accept the module with an ignore rule.

rules.summary: The module moved to another coordinate
rules.explanation: A relocation sends a dependency to another group. Check that the new owner is who you expect.

rules.summary: The POM declares its own repository
rules.explanation: A dependency that brings its own repository can pull later versions from anywhere.
